script: In the first years of life, a child's brain builds a million new connections every second. Here's how. At birth, a baby already has nearly all its neurons — eighty-six billion of them. But they're barely connected. Then, the explosion. By age three, the brain holds a thousand trillion connections — twice as many as yours. That's why toddlers absorb three languages at once — and you struggle to finish one app. But here's the strange part. Around age ten, the brain begins deleting itself. Unused connections are pruned away — almost half of them. Use it, or lose it. What survives gets faster — wrapped in fatty insulation called myelin, so signals travel ten times quicker. The last part to finish is the prefrontal cortex — the bit that plans, focuses, and stops bad decisions. It isn't complete until age twenty-five. But brains don't wire themselves. Every conversation, every game of peek-a-boo, every story read aloud decides which connections survive. Neglect decides too. Because in the first years, a child's brain builds a million connections a second — and it's waiting for you.
